title: Turn clinic note bullets into a GP letter
whyItWorks: Naming the convention and the length stops it waffling. The "do not invent" line cuts hallucination on meds and tests, which is the dangerous failure mode here.
watchOut: Always read the whole letter before sending. Drug doses and follow-up intervals are the two things to double check every time.
exampleOutput:
Dear Dr Smith,

Mr Jones was seen in clinic today with stable angina, well controlled on current treatment.

Plan for you:
- Continue current medication, review in 6 months
- Repeat lipid profile before next review
- [TO CONFIRM] whether a recent ECG is available

With thanks,

title: Summarise a discharge summary for a busy clinic
whyItWorks: The three-section frame matches how clinicians actually read a discharge. Asking for old and new dose surfaces the most common transcription error.
watchOut: Strip identifiers before pasting, whichever Copilot you use, and follow your trust's IG policy. Sign in with your work account, never a personal one, so enterprise data protection applies.
exampleOutput:
1) Admitted with a chest infection, treated and now stable for discharge.
2) Medication changes:
- Amlodipine increased from 5mg to 10mg
- Course of antibiotics added for 5 days
3) Follow-up:
- GP to recheck blood pressure in 2 weeks (GP)
- Chest clinic review in 6 weeks (hospital)

title: Draft a plain-English patient info leaflet
prompt: Write a patient information leaflet about {topic}. Reading age 11. UK English. Around 350 words. Use these sections: What this is. Why we think you need it. What it involves on the day. Common side effects. Less common but serious side effects. Who to call if you are worried. Use plain words. No medical jargon unless you explain it in brackets.
whyItWorks: Specifying reading age 11 and naming the sections gives it the structure NHS leaflets actually use, without the corporate tone.
watchOut: Get clinical sign-off before you give this to a patient. Treat the output as a first draft, never a final.
exampleOutput:
What this is
A small camera test that looks at the inside of your tummy.

Why we think you need it
To find out what is causing your symptoms.

What it involves on the day
You will be asked not to eat for six hours beforehand...

title: Pull actions out of MDT meeting notes
whyItWorks: Structured output as a table is what Copilot is genuinely good at. The unassigned flag forces the meeting chair to chase up the gaps.
watchOut: Patient initials only. Never paste full names or NHS numbers into a chat session that is not inside your tenant.
exampleOutput:
| Initials | Decision | Action | Owner |
| AB | For surgery | Add to list | Mr Patel |
| CD | Needs scan | Request MRI | [unassigned] |

Still open: CD, pending MRI before a plan can be agreed.

title: Compare two guidelines side by side
whyItWorks: Comparison tables are hard to keep in your head and easy to mess up by hand. Asking it to flag disagreements is the bit that actually saves you reading time.
watchOut: Sanity check the rows that disagree. Sometimes one guideline is silent rather than contradictory, and Copilot will sometimes confuse those.
exampleOutput:
| Row | Guideline A | Guideline B |
| First-line | Drug X | Drug X |
| Second-line | Drug Y | Drug Z |

Disagreement: A and B differ on second-line choice. B does not mention monitoring intervals.

title: Build a handover summary from shift notes
whyItWorks: SBAR is the format people already know. The "needs attention" prefix makes sure the urgent stuff is the first thing the next nurse reads.
watchOut: Read every line before passing on. Handover is the single most clinically risky bit of communication you do, and an LLM is not an authority on what matters.

title: Simplify a care plan for a family carer
prompt: Rewrite the care plan below for a family carer with no medical background. Reading age 11. UK English. Keep all the practical actions. Cut the jargon. Add a "what to watch for" section at the end with three things they should call the GP about.
whyItWorks: Care plans are written for clinicians but read by families. Asking it to keep the actions but cut the jargon does the translation work without losing the safety-net content.
watchOut: If the original plan has specific wording your service requires (legal or safeguarding), put it back in by hand. LLMs round those off.
exampleOutput:
Every morning, help with washing and dressing. Give the morning tablets with breakfast.

What to watch for, call the GP if:
- The wound looks red or hot
- A new high temperature
- Much less eating or drinking than usual

title: Outline a training pack on a new procedure
prompt: Outline a 45-minute training session on {topic} for a mixed audience of nurses and HCAs. Include: aims, three learning outcomes phrased as "by the end you will be able to...", a 5-minute icebreaker, the main teaching block with timings, a 10-minute practical, and three questions you would ask to check understanding.
whyItWorks: Asking for timings and check questions forces it to think about pacing rather than just listing topics.
watchOut: It will sometimes invent clinical detail in the practical section. Replace those bits with your own kit list and steps.
exampleOutput:
Aim: confident, safe use of the new device.
Outcomes: by the end you will be able to set it up, run a check, and spot a fault.
Icebreaker (5 min): one thing that goes wrong now.
Teaching (20 min)... Practical (10 min)... Check questions (3).

title: Draft survey questions for a small ward audit
prompt: Draft 10 survey questions to audit {topic} on a 24-bed ward. Mix closed (Likert 1 to 5) and open. Avoid leading questions. Group into three sections. UK English.
whyItWorks: The mix and the leading-questions rule are what stop the survey returning a meaningless 4.7 out of 5 score.
watchOut: Run the questions past one or two colleagues before sending. Surveys feel small but bad ones eat ward time.
exampleOutput:
Section 1, your experience:
1. How clear was the information you were given? (1 to 5)
2. What is one thing we could have explained better? (open)

Section 2, the environment... Section 3, overall...

title: Triage a backlog of clinic emails
prompt: Look at my unread emails from the last seven days. For each one, give me: subject, who from, one-line summary, and a recommended action from this list: Reply today, Reply this week, FYI no reply, Forward to {name}, Archive. Sort with "Reply today" at the top.
whyItWorks: Constraining the action to a short list is the bit that turns a vague summary into a workable list. M365 Copilot can actually read your inbox, which is the only reason this prompt works.
watchOut: It only sees emails your account can see. If you have shared mailboxes set up oddly, double check the scope before trusting the list.

title: Minutes from a Teams transcript
prompt: Produce minutes from the Teams meeting transcript {link or paste}. Sections: Attendees, Apologies, Decisions, Actions with owner and due date, Next meeting. Use UK English. Keep direct quotes only where they affect a decision.
whyItWorks: Teams transcripts are messy. Naming the sections gives it a shape to fit the noise into.
watchOut: Owners and dates are the two things to verify by hand. The transcript often does not contain them and Copilot will guess.
exampleOutput:
Attendees: ...
Apologies: ...
Decisions: agreed to move the clinic to Tuesdays.
Actions: update the rota (Tom, by Fri 14th); tell patients (Sara, by Mon 17th).
Next meeting: first Monday next month.

title: Spot clashes in a draft rota
whyItWorks: Rota maths is exactly the kind of fiddly logic an LLM can do reliably if you tell it the rules. The explicit rules are doing the work.
watchOut: Always paste the rota in a clean tabular format. If columns drift, the analysis goes wrong silently.
exampleOutput:
Issues found:
- 12 Mar: J. Doe has only 9 hours between a late and an early.
- 14 Mar: night shift has nobody assigned.
- 15 Mar: A. Khan is scheduled during booked annual leave.

title: Personalise a standard response letter
whyItWorks: Templates exist for a reason. Telling it not to touch the clinical content keeps it from "improving" things that need to stay exact.
watchOut: Spot-check the name and the date. Those are the bits that most embarrass you if they go wrong.
exampleOutput:
Dear Mrs Ahmed,

Your appointment is confirmed for Tuesday 18 March at 10:15 in the Cardiology clinic.

[the rest of the template, unchanged]

title: Build an agenda from a one-line brief
prompt: Draft an agenda for a 60-minute meeting on {topic} with {attendees}. Include timings per item, owner per item, and a 5-minute slot at the end for actions and ownership. UK English. No more than 6 substantive items.
whyItWorks: The cap of six items stops it producing a bloated 14-item list. Timings per item force prioritisation.
watchOut: It does not know your politics. Sense-check who gets to own the first item.
exampleOutput:
1. Welcome and apologies (5 min, Chair)
2. Last actions (10 min, Chair)
3. Main topic (25 min, Lead)
4. Risks (10 min, all)
5. AOB (5 min)
6. Actions and owners (5 min, Chair)

title: Reconcile a supplier statement against ledger
whyItWorks: A finite "likely cause" list keeps it from inventing categories. Sorting by absolute difference puts the worst rows at the top, where they belong.
watchOut: Always reconcile the totals manually before trusting the line-by-line. If totals do not match what you pasted, the paste is the bug.

title: Write a budget variance narrative
whyItWorks: Explicitly banning filler phrases gets you commentary that reads like a person wrote it. Naming the format saves a round of rewriting.
watchOut: Cross-check the numbers it quotes. LLMs can transpose digits when pasted figures are dense.
exampleOutput: Surgery is 120k overspent year to date, driven by pay (agency cover for two vacancies) rather than non-pay, which is on plan. Recruitment to both posts is expected to close the gap by Q3.

title: Generate cost improvement ideas for a service line
prompt: I run finance for {service line, e.g. outpatient ophthalmology} in a UK trust. Suggest 10 cost improvement ideas. For each: one-line description, rough size of saving (small, medium, large), main risk, and what evidence I would need to make the case. UK English. Avoid generic ideas like "go paperless".
whyItWorks: The "avoid generic" line genuinely changes the output. Asking for risk and evidence stops it pitching ideas the board would laugh at.
watchOut: Treat it as a brainstorm. None of these are vetted against your data.
exampleOutput:
1. Shift stable follow-ups to virtual (medium saving; risk: digital exclusion; evidence: DNA rates by mode).
2. Pool a shared injection list across consultants (small; risk: training; evidence: current per-list utilisation).

title: Extract coding details from an invoice batch
prompt: From the invoices in {folder name}, extract: Supplier, Invoice date, Net, VAT, Gross, Likely cost centre based on supplier name and description, Confidence (high, medium, low). Output as a CSV-ready table. Flag any with confidence "low" in a separate list at the bottom.
whyItWorks: Confidence-tagged extraction means you can split your time. Trust the highs, audit the lows.
watchOut: Test on a known batch first. The cost-centre mapping is only as good as the conventions in your supplier names.
exampleOutput:
Supplier,Date,Net,VAT,Gross,Cost centre,Confidence
Acme,03/02,1000,200,1200,Estates,high

Low confidence to review:
- Invoice 5567, supplier name unclear.

title: Draft an inclusive job description
prompt: Draft a job description for {role} at Band {x} in a UK trust. Sections: Role purpose, Key responsibilities (no more than 8 bullets), Essential skills, Desirable skills, About us (one paragraph). Avoid gendered language. Avoid jargon like "passionate" or "rockstar". UK English. Around 500 words.
whyItWorks: The word and bullet caps stop it producing an unreadable wall. The named bans on jargon save a rewrite.
watchOut: Run it past your EDI lead before posting. LLMs absorb the biases in their training data, which leans American.

title: Rewrite a policy into plain English
prompt: Rewrite the policy below in plain English. Reading age 13. Keep all the obligations and timelines. Cut the legalese. Where there is a specific timeline (e.g. "within 14 days"), keep it exactly. UK English. Use bullet points for any list of steps.
whyItWorks: Telling it to preserve timelines exactly is the safety check that lets you use the output without lawyering it again.
watchOut: If the policy quotes legislation, double check the quoted phrasing has not been "smoothed".
exampleOutput:
If you want to raise a grievance:
- Put it in writing to your manager.
- They must meet you within 14 days.
- You can bring a colleague or union rep.
- You will get a written outcome within 14 days of the meeting.

title: Build a competency-based interview pack
whyItWorks: Tying the questions back to the JD is the difference between a useful interview pack and a generic list of "tell me about a time" questions.
watchOut: Have at least one panel member review the rubric before you go live. Scoring rubrics drift if nobody owns them.
exampleOutput:
Q1 (competency, organising): Tell us about a time you managed competing deadlines.
Probes: what did you drop? what would you do differently?
Rubric: 1 no example, 4 clear example with reflection.

title: Summarise team absence trends
prompt: Look at the absence data attached. Summarise: total days lost this quarter vs last, top three reason categories, any individuals with more than {n} episodes, and any pattern by day of week. Output as short bullets. Do not name individuals, just initials.
whyItWorks: Asking for initials only sets the privacy ground rules in the prompt itself, rather than relying on you to redact after.
watchOut: Even initials can be identifying in a small team. If you forward the summary, swap initials for "Person A, Person B".
exampleOutput:
- Days lost: 84 this quarter, up from 71.
- Top reasons: coughs and colds, stress, musculoskeletal.
- More than 3 episodes: AB, CD.
- Pattern: Mondays slightly higher.

title: First draft of a DPIA for a low-risk tool
prompt: Draft a Data Protection Impact Assessment for {tool name}. Follow the ICO template structure. Sections: Description of processing, Necessity and proportionality, Risks (use a risk-likelihood-impact table), Measures to mitigate. UK English. Keep each section to under 250 words. Flag any sections where you would need information from the supplier with [SUPPLIER INPUT].
whyItWorks: The [SUPPLIER INPUT] flag turns the document into a list of questions for procurement, which is the part of DPIA work that always slips.
watchOut: A DPIA is a legal record. Treat any LLM output as a first draft only. The signatures at the bottom carry weight.

title: Draft a holding response to a SAR
prompt: Draft a holding response to a subject access request received today. UK GDPR conventions. Acknowledge receipt, set out the one-month timeline, ask for ID verification if not already provided, ask for any clarifications needed to narrow the scope. Polite, plain English. UK English.
whyItWorks: The four asks in one letter are what the ICO guidance actually expects. Pulling them together saves you a copy-paste from past responses.
watchOut: Check your trust template first. Local SAR teams often have wording they need exactly.
exampleOutput: Thank you for your request, received today. We will respond within one month. To proceed we need to verify your identity, please send one form of photo ID. It would also help if you could tell us which records or dates you are interested in.

title: Plain-English explainer of sensitivity labels
prompt: Explain Microsoft 365 sensitivity labels to a ward clerk. Three sections: What they are. What changes when you apply them. When you should stop and ask. Plain English. UK English. Around 250 words total. No jargon unless you explain it in brackets.
whyItWorks: A ward clerk is a real reader, not a marketing persona. The "when to stop and ask" section is the bit that actually changes behaviour.
watchOut: Your trust may have renamed the labels. Replace generic names with whatever yours uses before sharing.
exampleOutput:
What they are
A tag you put on a document or email to say how sensitive it is.

What changes
Some labels stop a file being sent outside the trust.

When to stop and ask
If you are unsure whether something counts as confidential, ask before you send.

title: Draft the narrative for a data incident report
whyItWorks: The "do not infer cause" instruction is the difference between a clean factual narrative and one that pre-empts the investigation.
watchOut: Incident reports are evidence. Print and keep the original prompt and output. Note them as a working draft only.
exampleOutput: At 09:14 an email containing a spreadsheet was sent to an external address. At 09:20 the sender noticed the error and recalled the message. At 09:35 the line manager was informed and the IG team was notified.

title: Write a RAG status report from project notes
whyItWorks: Forcing a one-line justification next to the RAG colour stops the status being a gut feeling. Separating "decisions needed" makes the report actionable rather than just informative.
watchOut: You own the RAG rating, not the model. If it calls something green that you know is amber, override it. Check every date against the plan.

title: Turn a brain-dump into a structured risk register
whyItWorks: The "cause leads to event leads to impact" phrasing turns vague worries into proper risk statements you can actually mitigate. Banning invented risks keeps the register honest.
watchOut: Likelihood and impact scores are a judgement call. Treat its numbers as a starting point and adjust them with the people who know the work.

title: Draft a project brief or PID skeleton
prompt: Draft the skeleton of a project brief for {project} in a UK trust. Sections: background, objectives, scope (in and explicitly out), key deliverables, milestones as [DATE], dependencies, assumptions, high-level risks, and success measures. UK English. Mark anything I need to supply with [...]. Keep it a structured skeleton, not waffle.
whyItWorks: Forcing an explicit "out of scope" list is the single most useful thing a brief can do, and it is the bit people forget. The placeholders turn it into a fill-in-the-blanks job.
watchOut: Scope is political. Get the sponsor to sign off the in and out lists before you circulate, not after.

title: Build a stakeholder map and engagement plan
whyItWorks: Surfacing the high-influence sceptics as a named priority is exactly where a PM should spend their time. The "what they need from me" column turns a map into a plan.
watchOut: Stances are sensitive. Keep this file off shared drives and never paste real names into the free Copilot Chat tier.

title: Pull actions and chase owners after a meeting
whyItWorks: Doing the extraction and the chaser email in one pass is the real time saver. The [TBC] flags stop it quietly inventing owners and deadlines.
watchOut: Read the action wording before sending. A transcript often records a half-formed idea as a firm commitment.

title: Run a structured lessons learned review
whyItWorks: Banning platitudes like "improve communication" is what forces genuinely usable lessons. Tying each to an owner stops the review being filed and forgotten.
watchOut: Anonymise the notes if the retro was candid. People stop being honest if they think their words will be attributed.

title: Draft a benefits realisation plan
whyItWorks: Splitting cashable from non-cashable benefits is what finance and the board actually want to see. The [BASELINE] flags show you what you need to measure before go-live, not after.
watchOut: A benefit with no baseline cannot be proven later. Capture the [BASELINE] figures before the project changes anything.

title: Turn a detailed plan into a plan on a page
prompt: Summarise the detailed project plan below into a plan on a page for a senior audience. UK English. Show the key phases, the three or four headline milestones with dates, the critical path in one line, and the top three risks. Cut the task-level detail. Keep every date exactly as given, do not round or shift them.
whyItWorks: Senior readers want the shape, not the Gantt. Telling it to keep dates exactly stops the summary quietly drifting from the real plan.
watchOut: Check that the milestones it picked are the ones that actually matter to the board, not just the nearest ones.

title: Draft a PRINCE2 exception report
whyItWorks: Laying out options with pros and cons, then a clear recommendation, is exactly what a board needs to give a fast direction. Naming which tolerance is breached keeps it true to PRINCE2.
watchOut: The recommendation is yours to own. Sense-check that the option you are recommending is one the board can actually authorise within their delegation.

title: Draft a PRINCE2 business case outline
prompt: Draft the outline of a PRINCE2 business case for {project} in a UK trust. Sections: executive summary, reasons, business options (including do nothing and do minimum), expected benefits, expected dis-benefits, timescale, costs, investment appraisal, and major risks. UK English. Mark every figure I must supply with [FIGURE]. Keep it a structured outline, not prose.
whyItWorks: Forcing do nothing and do minimum as options is what makes a PRINCE2 business case credible to a board. The explicit dis-benefits section is the bit most drafts skip.
watchOut: Do not let it populate the [FIGURE] markers. Costs and benefits are yours to source from real data, never the model.

title: Draft an end stage report for stage boundary
whyItWorks: Reporting tolerances actually used against those agreed is the heart of stage control. Ending on a clear proceed or hold recommendation is what the board needs at a stage boundary.
watchOut: Be honest about tolerances consumed. A rosy end stage report that hides slippage just moves the problem into the next stage.

title: Write a PRINCE2 product description
prompt: Write a PRINCE2 product description for {product}. UK English. Sections: purpose, composition, derivation (what it is based on), format and presentation, who produces it, quality criteria (specific and measurable), quality method, and who approves it. Keep the quality criteria testable, not vague. Mark anything I need to confirm with [...].
whyItWorks: Testable quality criteria are the whole point of a product description, and they are the bit teams fudge. Forcing measurable criteria up front saves an argument at the quality review.
watchOut: Check the quality criteria can really be tested. "User-friendly" is not a criterion, "passes WCAG 2.2 AA" is.

title: Build a checkpoint report from team updates
whyItWorks: Pulling scattered team updates into one checkpoint with a tolerance view is what lets a PM manage by exception. The [TOLERANCE] flag surfaces trouble before it becomes an exception.
watchOut: Confirm the tolerance figures with the team lead. The model can only flag what the updates actually mention.

title: Draft a work package to hand to a team
prompt: Draft a PRINCE2 work package for {piece of work}. UK English. Cover: the products to be delivered with their quality criteria, the agreed tolerances (time, cost, scope), constraints, interfaces and dependencies, how progress should be reported and how often, and how the work will be approved. Mark anything I must confirm with [...]. Keep it practical, this goes to a team to act on.
whyItWorks: Stating tolerances and reporting frequency in the work package is what lets you delegate and then manage by exception. The approval method removes the "is it done?" argument later.
watchOut: Agree the tolerances with the team before you issue this, not after. A work package handed down without buy-in tends to bounce straight back.

title: Draft a major incident update for users
prompt: Draft a service status update for staff about {incident}. UK English. Calm, clear, no blame, no jargon. Cover: what is affected, what is not, what we are doing, the workaround if there is one, and when the next update will come. Keep under 120 words. Do not speculate on cause or fix time beyond what I tell you.
whyItWorks: Telling it not to speculate on cause or fix time is what keeps you out of trouble during a live incident. The "next update" promise is what stops the service desk being flooded.
watchOut: Get the on-call lead to approve before it goes trust-wide. Incident comms are scrutinised afterwards, so keep a copy of what you sent and when.

title: Summarise a long ticket thread for handover
whyItWorks: A clean handover summary is the difference between a five-minute pickup and re-reading forty updates. Naming the single next step stops the new person retreading old ground.
watchOut: Scrub any passwords, tokens or personal data out of the thread before pasting into the free Copilot Chat tier.

title: Draft a runbook from a fix you just did
whyItWorks: A verify step and a rollback are what separate a runbook from a note to self. Telling it not to tidy commands stops it silently breaking your syntax.
watchOut: Test the runbook on a non-live system before trusting it. Commands the model has reformatted can fail in subtle ways.

title: Write up a change request for CAB
prompt: Draft a change request for the change advisory board. UK English. Cover: what is changing and why, the systems and users affected, the implementation plan in steps, the test plan, the rollback plan, the risk if we do nothing, and the proposed window. Mark anything needing a real figure or date with [...]. Be concise, CAB reads a lot of these.
whyItWorks: A clear rollback plan and a stated "risk of doing nothing" are the two things CAB approvals hinge on. Writing them up front speeds the whole thing through.
watchOut: The rollback plan is the one section never to fudge. If you cannot describe how to undo it, the change is not ready.

title: Explain an unfamiliar script before you run it
whyItWorks: Getting a plain-English read before you run an inherited script catches the destructive line you would otherwise miss. The safety flags at the end are the bit that saves you.
watchOut: The explanation is a second opinion, not a guarantee. Never run something against production on the strength of an LLM read alone.

title: Turn an IT policy into a plain-English staff notice
prompt: Rewrite the IT policy below as a short notice for non-technical staff. UK English. Plain language. Tell them what is changing, what they need to do, by when, and who to contact if stuck. Keep any hard security requirement exact, do not soften it. Under 200 words.
whyItWorks: Staff ignore policy PDFs but read a short notice that tells them what to actually do. Keeping the hard security requirement exact stops the plain-English version becoming wrong.
watchOut: Check it has not relaxed a "must" into a "should". Security wording is where paraphrasing does real damage.

title: Clean and standardise a messy asset list
whyItWorks: Normalising device types to a fixed set is what makes the data reportable. Surfacing duplicate tags catches the errors that break an asset audit.
watchOut: Spot-check the normalisation. The model can misclassify an all-in-one or a docking station, so eyeball the "other" rows.

title: Decode a vendor email and draft a reply
prompt: Read the vendor email below. UK English. Tell me in plain English: what they are actually asking or telling me, anything that commits us to cost or action, any deadline, and anything that sounds like upsell dressed up as a requirement. Then draft a short, firm reply that asks for the two or three things I would need to make a decision.
whyItWorks: Separating a genuine requirement from upsell dressed up as one is the read most IT teams want from vendor mail. Drafting the clarifying reply in the same pass saves a round trip.
watchOut: Do not let the draft commit to anything. Check it asks questions rather than agreeing to spend or timelines.

title: Turn an executive inbox into a daily action list
prompt: Go through my director's unread emails from the last two days. For each, give: who from, one-line summary, and a recommended action from this list: needs them today, I can handle, needs a reply this week, FYI only, decline politely. Group by recommended action with "needs them today" at the top. Flag anything that looks time sensitive or from a named VIP.
whyItWorks: Splitting "I can handle" from "needs them today" is the core of the EA job, and a fixed action list keeps the triage consistent. Flagging VIPs stops the one email that matters slipping down the pile.
watchOut: It only sees mailboxes the account can access. Check delegate access is set up correctly before trusting the sweep, and never let it auto-send.

title: Find and untangle diary clashes
prompt: Look at my director's calendar for next week. List any clashes, any meetings with no agenda or no location, any day with no break longer than 30 minutes between 9 and 5, and any back-to-back meetings across different sites with no travel time. For each issue, suggest a fix. UK English.
whyItWorks: Catching no travel time between sites and no breaks is exactly the protective work a good EA does. Asking for a suggested fix turns a list of problems into a list of decisions.
watchOut: It does not know which meetings are immovable. Treat its suggested moves as drafts and confirm priorities before rearranging anything.

title: Build a pre-meeting brief for your exec
prompt: My director has a meeting with {person or group} on {date}. Pull together a one-page brief: who they are meeting and their role, the purpose, the last few emails or documents exchanged, any outstanding actions on either side, and three things my director should know walking in. UK English. Keep it to one page.
whyItWorks: A one-page brief is what lets an exec walk into a meeting prepared in two minutes. Surfacing outstanding actions on both sides is the detail that makes them look on top of it.
watchOut: It can miss context shared verbally or in chats it cannot see. Add anything you know that the email trail does not capture.

title: Draft a clean travel itinerary from booking emails
whyItWorks: A single time-ordered itinerary beats forwarding six confirmation emails. The [TIGHT] flag catches the connection that will cause a panicked call from a station.
watchOut: Double-check the times against the original bookings, especially anything crossing midnight or a timezone.

title: Draft a reply in your executive’s voice
prompt: Draft a reply on behalf of my director to the email below. UK English. Match this style: {warm but brief / formal / direct}. The reply should: {what you want it to do}. Sign off as [NAME]. Keep it short. Do not commit to dates or decisions I have not given you, flag those as [CONFIRM WITH DIRECTOR].
whyItWorks: Naming the house style and flagging anything that needs the exec’s sign-off lets you draft confidently without overstepping. The [CONFIRM] markers keep you on the right side of the line.
watchOut: Always have the director approve anything that commits them. Drafting in someone’s voice is a privilege that depends on never sending something they would not have said.

title: Check a board or committee pack is complete
whyItWorks: Cross-checking agenda items against papers is fiddly and easy to get wrong by hand the night before a board. Turning the gaps into a chaser list is the part that saves the evening.
watchOut: Confirm author names before sending chasers. The agenda does not always say who owns a missing paper.

title: Tidy rough minutes into a clean record
prompt: Tidy the rough minutes below into a clean record. UK English. Keep the house structure: present, apologies, items discussed with key points, decisions, and an action table with owner and due date. Keep it factual and neutral, cut the chat. Do not add decisions or actions that are not in my notes. Flag any action with no owner as [unassigned].
whyItWorks: Neutral, factual minutes are a skill, and the model is good at stripping the chat while keeping the decisions. The [unassigned] flag forces the chair to fill the gaps.
watchOut: You are the record keeper. Read every decision line carefully, because a tidied minute that subtly changes a decision causes real problems later.

title: Plan a realistic day around fixed commitments
whyItWorks: Protecting a focus block and being honest about what will not fit is what separates a plan from a wish list. Putting the priority task in the morning respects how people actually work.
watchOut: You know their rhythms better than the model. Adjust the energy assumptions to the person, some do their best thinking late.

title: Explain a tech change to a non-technical board
prompt: Explain {technical change} to a hospital board. No jargon. Three short paragraphs: What is changing. Why it matters to patient care. What you are asking the board to decide. UK English. Around 300 words.
whyItWorks: The "what you are asking the board to decide" framing is what boards actually want. Most papers forget to ask the question.
watchOut: Get the operations director to read it before you submit. Board readers spot vagueness instantly.

title: Tighten an email you have already written
whyItWorks: Asking it to keep your voice and not add content is what stops the output sounding like LinkedIn corporate.
watchOut: Read the output for tone. Sometimes "tightening" removes a polite hedge that was doing diplomatic work.
exampleOutput:
Before: I was just wondering if you might possibly have a moment at some point to look over the attached when you get a chance.

After: Could you review the attached by Friday? Thanks.

title: Translate clinical jargon for a colleague in a different team
prompt: Explain {clinical term or process} to a colleague in {their team, e.g. finance, IT}. One paragraph. Tell them what it is, why it matters to their work, and the one thing they would otherwise get wrong about it. UK English.
whyItWorks: The "what they would otherwise get wrong" frame is the difference between a definition and a useful explanation.
watchOut: If the term has a strict regulatory meaning (Caldicott, Section 251), do not let it paraphrase. Quote the source.
exampleOutput: An RTT pathway tracks the time from referral to treatment. It matters to finance because breaches carry a cost and affect reporting. The thing people get wrong: the clock can pause, so the raw date difference is not the waiting time.

title: Brief yourself for a meeting in 5 minutes
prompt: I have a meeting in 30 minutes with {person or team}. Find the last 5 emails and any shared documents between us. Tell me: outstanding actions on me, outstanding actions on them, anything I promised to follow up on, and a one-line summary of where we are.
whyItWorks: This is the prompt that justifies M365 Copilot existing. Without graph access, you cannot do it. With it, it takes 30 seconds.
watchOut: It can miss documents shared via links rather than attachments. Glance at recent files manually if the meeting is high stakes.
exampleOutput:
On me: send the revised budget (promised last Tuesday).
On them: confirm the room booking.
Follow up: I said I would check the leave dates.
Where we are: agreed the plan, waiting on final numbers.

title: Draft a referral letter to another specialty
prompt: Draft a referral letter to {specialty} from the notes below. UK English, standard NHS referral convention. Open with the reason for referral in one sentence. Include relevant history, current medication, and the specific question you want them to answer. End with your contact details as [YOUR DETAILS]. Keep under 250 words. Do not invent results or medications.
whyItWorks: Naming the specific question you want answered is the bit most referrals miss, and it is the bit that stops the letter bouncing back. The placeholder keeps it from inventing your details.
watchOut: Check the history it pulls through. It will sometimes promote an old, resolved problem into the active list.

title: Explain a procedure for informed consent
prompt: Write a plain-English explanation of {procedure} to support an informed consent conversation. Reading age 11. UK English. Cover: what it involves, the main benefits, the common risks, the serious risks, and the alternatives including doing nothing. Do not give any risk frequencies or percentages. Where one is needed, write [APPROVED LOCAL FIGURE].
whyItWorks: Structuring around benefits, common risks, serious risks and alternatives matches the Montgomery standard for consent. The [LOCAL FIGURE] flag stops it inventing complication rates.
watchOut: Check it against your approved patient information. Risk figures must come from your own service, never from the model. A clinician leads the consent conversation.

title: Turn ward round notes into a task list
whyItWorks: Grouping by when it needs doing, not by patient, matches how a shift actually runs. The [DR] flag separates what you can crack on with from what needs escalating.
watchOut: Bed numbers move. Confirm the board before you action anything time critical.

title: Draft a falls or pressure risk assessment narrative
prompt: From the observations below, draft the narrative for a {falls / pressure area} risk assessment. Stick to the facts given. UK English. Use the structure: current risk factors, protective factors, interventions already stated in the notes, review date as [DATE]. Do not suggest new interventions. Do not invent a score. Do not infer mobility you were not told about.
whyItWorks: Telling it not to invent a score keeps the clinical judgement where it belongs, with you. The structure matches what most trust assessment tools expect.
watchOut: The score and the review date are yours to set. The model drafts the prose around them, nothing more.

title: Draft a sensitive update message for a family
prompt: Help me draft a short, warm message updating a family on {situation}. UK English. Calm and human, not clinical. Avoid false reassurance. Include one clear next step and how to reach the ward. Keep under 120 words. Leave the specifics I have not given you as [...].
whyItWorks: Asking it to avoid false reassurance is what keeps the tone honest. The word limit forces it to be kind without rambling.
watchOut: Read it aloud before sending. Tone is everything here, and what reads fine on screen can land wrong with a worried family.

title: Draft a waiting list update letter
prompt: Draft a letter updating a patient on their position on the {procedure} waiting list. UK English, warm but factual. Acknowledge the wait, explain what happens next, give the number to call to change contact details, and avoid promising a date. Keep under 200 words. Leave specifics as [...].
whyItWorks: Telling it not to promise a date keeps you out of trouble. The "what happens next" framing answers the question patients actually have.
watchOut: Check your PTL wording. Trusts often have approved phrasing for waiting list comms that has to be used exactly.

title: Turn a messy list into a clean spreadsheet
whyItWorks: Naming the columns and banning guesses turns unstructured text into something you can paste straight into Excel. The [blank] marker shows you exactly where the gaps are.
watchOut: Spot-check a few rows against the source. If the original formatting is wildly inconsistent, fields can land in the wrong column.

title: Write a polite chaser without sounding annoyed
prompt: Draft a short, polite chaser email about {outstanding thing}. This is the {first / second / third} time of asking. UK English. Firm but friendly, no passive aggression. State what I need, by when, and offer to help if there is a blocker. Under 90 words.
whyItWorks: Telling it which chase this is sets the firmness without you having to think about it. The offer to help keeps the relationship intact.
watchOut: On a third chase, read the tone carefully. The model tends to stay too soft when the situation needs a gentle escalation.

title: Summarise a finance pack for non-finance readers
prompt: Summarise the finance pack below for a clinical director with no finance background. UK English. Three short paragraphs: where we are against budget, the two things driving the variance, and the one decision we need from them. Use the figures verbatim. No jargon, no "favourable" or "adverse" without plain wording alongside.
whyItWorks: Asking it to translate "favourable" and "adverse" is what makes the summary land with a clinician. Naming the one decision stops it being a wall of numbers.
watchOut: Verify every figure it quotes against the pack. Dense tables are exactly where digit transposition creeps in.

title: Draft the skeleton of a business case
prompt: Draft the skeleton of a business case for {proposal} in a UK trust. Sections: problem, options appraisal (including do nothing), preferred option, costs and savings over 3 years, risks, benefits realisation. UK English. Mark every figure I need to supply with [FIGURE]. Keep it a skeleton, not prose.
whyItWorks: The [FIGURE] markers turn the output into a checklist of what you still need to gather. Forcing a do-nothing option is what makes a business case credible.
watchOut: Do not let it populate the numbers. Every [FIGURE] is yours to fill from real data, not the model.

title: Explain a purchase order query to a budget holder
whyItWorks: Budget holders ignore finance jargon. Naming the single action they need to take is what actually gets the PO released.
watchOut: Make sure it has not softened a hard requirement. If approval is mandatory, the email needs to say so plainly.

title: Prepare for a difficult conversation
prompt: Help me prepare for a difficult conversation about {issue} with a team member. UK English. Give me: a calm opening line, three things to keep the focus on behaviour not character, two likely reactions and how to respond, and a constructive way to close. This is preparation, not a script to read out.
whyItWorks: Anticipating likely reactions is the part people skip and then get caught out by. Keeping focus on behaviour not character is the single most useful framing for these talks.
watchOut: If the issue touches conduct, capability or anything formal, involve HR before you have the conversation, not after.

title: Write a recruitment advert from a job description
whyItWorks: Leading with why someone would want the job, not the duties, is what separates an advert that gets applicants from one that gets ignored. The banned cliches save a rewrite.
watchOut: Check it has carried the essential criteria through accurately. Adverts that misstate requirements cause shortlisting headaches later.

title: Pull themes out of exit interview notes
whyItWorks: Asking for paraphrases not quotes protects anonymity in a small team. Pulling out single safeguarding concerns separately stops them being averaged away in the themes.
watchOut: Anonymise the notes before pasting. Exit interviews are candid and easily identifying.

title: Draft a plain answer to a staff IG question
prompt: A member of staff has asked: "{question}". Draft a plain-English answer. UK English. Tell them the short answer first, then the reason, then where to go if they need a decision in writing. Do not overstate certainty. If the honest answer is "it depends", say so and name what it depends on.
whyItWorks: Leading with the short answer respects the asker. Letting it say "it depends" stops it inventing a false black-and-white rule.
watchOut: IG answers carry weight. If the question touches a real decision, route it through your formal advice process rather than sending the draft as gospel.

title: Build a checklist before sharing data externally
prompt: I have been asked to share {dataset} with {organisation} for {purpose}. Build a pre-share checklist. UK English. Cover: lawful basis, minimisation, is there a data sharing agreement, how it will be transferred securely, retention and deletion, and who signs it off. Flag anything I would need legal or DPO input on with [DPO].
whyItWorks: Turning the share into a checklist catches the steps people skip under time pressure. The [DPO] flags show exactly where to stop and ask.
watchOut: A checklist is a prompt to think, not a sign-off. Do not share anything externally on the strength of this alone.

title: Explain a records retention rule in plain English
prompt: Explain the retention rule for {record type} to a team that wants to delete things to save space. UK English. Plain language. Tell them how long it must be kept, why, what counts as the start of the clock, and what to do when the period ends. Note that you are summarising and they should confirm against the Records Management Code.
whyItWorks: Naming when the retention clock starts is the detail teams get wrong most often. The explicit "confirm against the Code" line keeps the summary honest.
watchOut: Retention periods change. Always check the current Records Management Code of Practice rather than trusting a remembered figure.

title: Get tough but fair feedback on a document
whyItWorks: Casting it as a sceptical, time-poor reader gets you the critique you would otherwise only find out about in the meeting. Banning padding keeps the feedback useful.
watchOut: It cannot judge accuracy of facts it cannot check. Treat it as a reader of structure and clarity, not a fact checker.

title: Turn scrappy notes into a status update
whyItWorks: The done / in progress / blocked structure is what managers scan for. "Do not invent progress" keeps you honest when the notes are thin.
watchOut: Check the blocked section names a real ask. The model sometimes states a problem without the request that goes with it.

title: Pressure-test a decision before you commit
prompt: I am about to decide to {decision}. Play devil's advocate. UK English. Give me the strongest three arguments against, the assumption I am most likely getting wrong, what would have to be true for this to fail, and one cheaper way to test it first. Be blunt.
whyItWorks: Asking for a cheap test first is the question that saves the most money. Naming the shaky assumption surfaces the risk you have stopped seeing.
watchOut: It argues whatever side you ask it to. Use it to stress-test your own thinking, not to outsource the call.

title: Decode an email full of acronyms
whyItWorks: Flagging the acronyms it is unsure of with [?] is what stops it guessing and quietly misleading you. Useful for anyone new to a trust.
watchOut: Local acronyms vary between trusts. The [?] flags are where you will need a colleague who knows the patch.
